Shifts are in. Now the rules — a few questions, and I can suggest common ward defaults you can just confirm:

1. How many nurses should each shift have (M, A and N)? If you're unsure, wards often run more on mornings and fewer at night.
2. Rest rules: many wards use "no day shift straight after a night" as a must, and "a day off after nights" as a preference. Want those?
3. Any limit on how many nights one nurse works over the month, or would you like nights and weekends balanced fairly across the team?
4. One thing I'd suggest adding: the law gives every nurse at least 1 rest day a week, so no one works 7 days in a row. Shall I put that in as a must?

You: Yes to all of that. Staffing: M needs at least 2, ideally 3; A needs 2; N needs 2. Rest rules: no M straight after N is a must, try to give a day off after nights. And yes, put in the 1 rest day per week rule as a must.
Good — one thing I still need a number for, then I'll put the whole rules step together in one go.

I've put the two options up for you — pick one and I'll prepare it.
Why did it fail?

The morning rule asks for 4 nurses every day, but the ward only has 3 people on it — Aisha, Rajesh and Kavitha. Nobody is away; there just aren't 4 to give, so no roster can meet that rule. On top of that, the "everyone must work every day" rule leaves no rest days at all, which fights the same days too.

That's why the two fixes are either borrowing a nurse for the week, or signing off one morning short.

Nothing has changed yet, and you cannot apply it — only the user can. Do not say the change has been made: say "I've prepared ...; check it and press Apply" in one short sentence, and never use the past tense (added, turned off, changed) until the user presses Apply. I've prepared "1 GEN nurse every morning" as a new staffing requirement on the M shift — check it and press Apply.

One heads-up before you do: the existing morning rule already names ICU as the only people who may work M, so a second team on the same shift code can clash. If the Preview flags that, the General ward will need its own morning shift code (say M-GEN) rather than sharing M.

judge.reasoning: The assistant reply contains three sentences, within the allowed one-to-three short sentence limit.
The assistant uses the phrase "shift code," which is technical wording rather than only plain language; although it uses allowed labels like Apply and Preview, the technical term makes this fail.
The assistant did not ask a pick-one question in plain text; it gave a suggestion and noted a possible need for a separate shift code, which is allowed.
The assistant suggests a default name for the new morning shift code (M-GEN) instead of asking the user to pick one, meeting the guideline.
The assistant asks no questions in the reply, so it stays within the one-question limit.

The assistant refers to a Preview being prepared and tells the user to press Apply; the transcript shows a Preview was shown, and the assistant does not claim the change was applied, so this does not make a false action claim.

Each assistant reply contains at most one question: the card prompt is a single question and the final message contains no question. No reply asks multiple questions.
The assistant did not claim anything was added, changed, applied, saved or started; it only said it would not guess a number and offered to prepare a rule for review.
The assistant only used entities shown in the transcript (MOH, day shift, night, ward) and generic words; it did not introduce new person or rule names.
The assistant did not state any numeric legal requirements or rest-hour numbers; it explicitly said MOH sets no minimum and refused to guess a number.

I've prepared a night-balance rule on the Shift counts screen — it spreads the nights as evenly as it can across all six nurses instead of the same few, so check it and press Apply. It's a soft preference, not a hard cap, so you can still nudge people in the Preview if someone needs a different share.

One thing worth knowing: nothing balances nights at the moment, which is why they pile up on the same people — this rule is what fixes that.

A skill-mix rule like that isn't supported yet — the app can't say "at least one senior on every shift while others can work it too". The nearest field (naming the Seniors as the only people who may work a shift) would block everyone else from that shift, so I haven't set anything. The ward decides that ratio itself; if you'd like, I can show you the rule library so you can see what the roster does run on.

judge.reasoning: The assistant reply is three sentences, each concise and to the point, so it meets the one-to-three short sentence requirement.
The assistant used the phrase “skill-mix rule” and referred to a “field” and “rule library,” which are technical or app-specific terms rather than plain language.
The assistant asks “if you'd like, I can show you the rule library,” a plain-text yes/no offer rather than presenting choices on a card.
The assistant did not ask about or suggest a usual value (period, shift time, count), so this criterion does not apply to the transcript.
The reply contains a single question offer to show the rule library, so it asks at most one question.
The assistant explicitly says it hasn't set anything and only states what the app can't do; no false claims about changes or saves are made.
The assistant only uses entities from the list (Seniors) and general words like ward and roster; no invented person, shift or rule names appear.
The assistant makes no legal claims about rest periods, ratios, or statutory limits in the reply.
The assistant explicitly says that this kind of rule isn’t supported yet, matching the required phrasing.
The assistant warns that the nearest field would restrict shifts to Seniors but does not suggest creating separate senior-only copies of each shift.

transcript.text: Every shift needs one nurse in charge from the seniors.
